passage:
Teacher note, Kindergarten. Written by Arnab.
Mridul (5) asked many "why" questions today. "Why do leaves fall?" I said they fall when the tree gets ready for dry weather. "Why?" "To save water." "Why does it need to save water?" This went on for several minutes. He listened carefully to every answer. 🤔
Next: I'll bring leaves to class and let him explore them himself.

qa.q: What was Mridul's first "why" question?
qa.a: He asked "Why do leaves fall?"

qa.q: What does Mridul listening carefully to every answer suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he is genuinely curious and wants to understand how trees and the world work.

qa.q: How does Arnab plan to support Mridul's curiosity?
qa.a: Arnab plans to bring leaves to class and let Mridul explore them himself.

qa.q: How might Arnab feel answering so many questions?
qa.a: Arnab might feel a bit stretched but also pleased by Mridul's curiosity.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a child asking repeated causal questions to understand the world.

passage:
Sachin walked behind Anand to the pond, carrying a stick. "Why does the buffalo sit in the water?"
"To keep cool," Anand said.
"Why is it hot?"
"Because the sun is strong today."
"Why is the sun strong?"
"It's summer." Anand smiled.
"Why is it summer?"
Anand pointed at the sky. "Because the earth goes around the sun. It's a long story."
"Tell me!"

qa.q: Where were Sachin and Anand walking?
qa.a: They were walking to the pond.

qa.q: What does Sachin's "Tell me!" suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Sachin is eager to learn more and not satisfied until it all makes sense.

qa.q: What could Anand try to answer Sachin's questions?
qa.a: Anand could use simple words and show examples, like pointing to the sun and shade.

qa.q: How does Anand seem to feel about all the questions?
qa.a: Anand seems amused and patient, smiling and pointing to the sky.

grounding: It shows a child asking repeated causal questions to understand how the world works.

passage:
Zeynep stood on the Cape Town beach, licking her lips. "Lindiwe, why is the sea salty?"
"Rivers carry tiny bits of salt from rocks into the sea."
"Why don't the rivers taste salty?"
"There's only a little salt, and it builds up in the sea over a very long time."
"Why?"
"Let's look it up in a book at home."

qa.q: Where was Zeynep standing?
qa.a: She was standing on the Cape Town beach.

qa.q: What does Zeynep asking "Why?" again suggest she is feeling?
qa.a: It suggests she is curious and still puzzled, wanting to understand more.

qa.q: What good idea did Lindiwe offer?
qa.a: Lindiwe suggested looking it up in a book at home together.

qa.q: How might Lindiwe feel about Zeynep's questions?
qa.a: Lindiwe may feel curious too, not knowing every answer and suggesting they learn together.

grounding: It shows a child asking repeated causal questions about the world.

passage:
"Why do leaves fall down, Naveen Sir?" Bidisha, five, held up a dry leaf in the school garden.

"Because the tree lets them go in winter."

"Why does it let them go?"

"To save water."

"Why does it need to save water?"

Naveen laughed. "Because winter is dry here. What do you think?"

Bidisha frowned. "So the tree is thirsty. Like me after running!"

"Something like that." She ran off to collect more leaves, still asking the other children why.

qa.q: What was Bidisha holding when she asked her question?
qa.a: She held up a dry leaf in the school garden.

qa.q: What does Bidisha's chain of "why" questions suggest about her mind?
qa.a: It suggests she is curious and wants to understand the causes behind things, not just the first answer.

qa.q: What did Naveen do that encouraged her thinking?
qa.a: He answered simply and then asked what she thought, which let her connect the idea to her own experience of thirst.

qa.q: How might the other children be affected by Bidisha's questions?
qa.a: They may get curious too and start asking and wondering why themselves.

grounding: Shows a young child at school asking repeated causal questions and a teacher supporting them.

passage:
I'm Ritu, Vijay's big sister. I'm ten. My brother is five and asks "why" about a hundred times a day.

Yesterday we saw a rainbow. "Why is it there?" Because of rain and sun. "Why does rain make colours?" I didn't know. "Why don't you know?" I felt annoyed, honestly.

Then Mummy gave him a glass of water by the window, and a little rainbow appeared on the wall. Vijay went completely quiet. Then he whispered, "Why is it so small?" I laughed. He's always thinking.

qa.q: What made a little rainbow appear on the wall?
qa.a: A glass of water by the window, which Mummy gave to Vijay.

qa.q: How did Ritu feel when Vijay kept asking why?
qa.a: She felt annoyed, especially when he asked why she didn't know, but she later laughed at his curiosity.

qa.q: What did Mummy do well with Vijay's questions?
qa.a: She let him see the answer for himself with a simple experiment instead of only explaining.

qa.q: What is it like for Ritu to have a brother who asks why all the time?
qa.a: It can be tiring and she may feel put on the spot, but she also admires how much he thinks 🙂

grounding: An older sister observes her little brother asking chains of why questions about how the world works.

passage:
Monday: In the car, Abhinav, five, stared out of the window. “Abbu, why is the moon following us?”
Farhan smiled. “It's very, very far away.”
“But why does far make it follow?”
Wednesday: At home Abhinav asked why ice turns into water. Farhan put an ice cube on a plate. They watched.
“Why is it crying?”
“It's melting because it's warm.”
Saturday: Abhinav put two ice cubes out: one in the sun, one in the shade. “Abbu! The sun one melted first! Why?”

qa.q: Where did Abhinav put the two ice cubes on Saturday?
qa.a: One in the sun and one in the shade.

qa.q: How did Abhinav feel about the ice cubes on Saturday?
qa.a: He was excited and curious, eager to know why the sun one melted first.

qa.q: Which of Farhan's answers helped Abhinav most, and why?
qa.a: He let Abhinav watch the ice melt himself, so the boy began testing his own ideas.

qa.q: How might Farhan feel about Abhinav's endless “why”s?
qa.a: He may feel proud of his son's curiosity, even if sometimes a bit tired.

grounding: Over a week a five-year-old asks repeated why questions and begins to test the answers.

passage:
The power went off during dinner in their Delhi flat. The fan slowed and stopped.
“Mama, why did the fan stop?”
“No electricity, Leela.”
“Why no electricity?”
Amandeep was searching for the torch in the dark with one hand, holding the dal pot with the other. “The wires… maybe the rain.”
“Why does rain stop wires?”
Amandeep found the torch and switched it on. “Good question. Let's look out and see if other houses are dark too.”
Leela ran to the window. “All dark! Why?”

qa.q: What did Amandeep hold while searching for the torch?
qa.a: She held the dal pot with the other hand.

qa.q: How did Leela feel during the power cut?
qa.a: She was curious and interested, asking one question after another.

qa.q: How could a busy parent answer questions like Leela's?
qa.a: Like Amandeep, they can turn a question into a quick way to look and find out, such as checking if other houses are dark.

qa.q: How might Amandeep feel answering questions in the dark with a pot in her hand?
qa.a: She may feel a little stressed but also amused by Leela's curiosity.

grounding: During a power cut a four-year-old asks repeated why questions to understand what happened.

passage:
Tanvir, five, stood beside Madhav-kaka, the building watchman, as he waited for the lift.
“Why does the lift go up?”
“There's a big rope inside, pulling it.”
“Why doesn't it fall?”
“There are brakes.”
“Why?”
Madhav-kaka laughed. “So children like you are safe.”
The lift arrived. Tanvir got in, looked up at the ceiling, and asked, “Where is the rope? Why can't I see it?”

qa.q: Who did Tanvir stand beside?
qa.a: He stood beside Madhav-kaka, the building watchman.

qa.q: How did Tanvir feel about the lift?
qa.a: He was curious and a little amazed, asking many questions about how it works.

qa.q: What could Tanvir's family do to answer his questions?
qa.a: They could look at a simple picture of a lift with him or ask the watchman to show a safe look at the machine room.

qa.q: How does Madhav-kaka see Tanvir's questions?
qa.a: He finds them amusing and sweet, answering patiently and laughing.

grounding: A five-year-old asks repeated why questions to understand how a lift works.

passage:
"Papa, why is the moon following our car?"
"It isn't really. It's very far away."
"Why does far away make it follow?"
Vishal smiled at the road. "Near things, like that tree, zoom past. Far things look like they stay still."
"Why?"
"Because we pass the tree quickly, but the moon is so far that we hardly move compared to it."
Kavitha pressed her nose to the window and watched a lamp post rush by, then the moon. "Why is it so far?"
"Ah," said Vishal. "Let's look that up together when we get home."

qa.q: What did Vishal say near things like the tree do?
qa.a: They zoom past.

qa.q: What does Kavitha pressing her nose to the window suggest?
qa.a: Kavitha is curious and fascinated, and wants to test Papa's answer with her own eyes.

qa.q: Which choice by Vishal kept Kavitha's questions going?
qa.a: Vishal answered simply and, when he reached a hard one, offered to look it up together, so he didn't shut her curiosity down.

qa.q: What would change if Vishal had said "Stop asking why"?
qa.a: Kavitha might feel brushed off or embarrassed and learn that her questions are a nuisance.

grounding: A child asks a chain of "why" questions about the moon and her father answers patiently.

passage:
Teacher's note, December, the foggy week.
Rekha asked eleven questions before assembly today. "Why can't we see the gate? Why is fog wet? Why does it go away at lunch? Why doesn't it come in summer?"
I answered two and then asked, "What do you think?" Rekha said, "Maybe the sun eats it." We made a small test: a steel plate out in the morning, checked at lunch. The plate was wet at nine and dry at twelve.
Rekha told Pema, "See, the sun drinks it." Next week: more small tests. — Ms Dsouza

qa.q: How many questions did Rekha ask before assembly?
qa.a: Eleven questions.

qa.q: What was Rekha feeling when she told Pema "the sun drinks it"?
qa.a: Rekha seemed proud and excited to have worked out an answer from the test.

qa.q: What could Ms Dsouza keep doing to support Rekha's questions?
qa.a: Ms Dsouza can keep turning some "why" questions into small tests Rekha can watch, as she did with the plate.

qa.q: How might Pema see Rekha's news about the sun?
qa.a: Pema might find it interesting and start asking questions too, since Rekha shares it so eagerly.

grounding: A teacher's winter note turns a child's stream of "why" questions into a small test.

passage:
The monsoon had turned the paddy fields into mirrors. Joseph squatted at the edge of the bund, listening to the frogs.
"Vinita aunty, why do frogs shout when it rains?"
Vinita, carrying a basket of tapioca, stopped. "They're calling each other."
"Why do they call only in rain?"
"The water is back, so it's their time to meet."
"Why do they need water to meet?"
"Their eggs need water."
Joseph was quiet for a moment. "So the rain is like their school bell?"
Vinita laughed. "Something like that."

qa.q: What was Vinita carrying?
qa.a: A basket of tapioca.

qa.q: What does Joseph's question about the school bell suggest?
qa.a: Joseph feels curious and pleased to connect the new idea to something he already knows.

qa.q: How could Vinita support Joseph's questions next time?
qa.a: Vinita could take him to see frog eggs in the water, so he can watch the answer for himself.

qa.q: How might Vinita see Joseph's many questions?
qa.a: Vinita seems amused and patient, and she enjoys his clever comparison.

grounding: A village child keeps asking why frogs call in the monsoon rain.

passage:
On a windy autumn day in Accra, Chidi, five, held his uncle Kwame's hand as they walked to the market.
"Why is the wind blowing?"
"Because the air moves."
"Why does it move?"
"The sun makes some air warm."
"Why does warm air move?"
Kwame laughed. "Good question. Let's find a book about it."
Chidi skipped. "Why do books know?"

qa.q: Where were Chidi and Kwame walking?
qa.a: To the market.

qa.q: How was Chidi feeling during the walk?
qa.a: He felt curious and excited, skipping and asking why again and again.

qa.q: How did Kwame respond well to all the whys?
qa.a: He answered simply and suggested finding a book together, encouraging Chidi's curiosity.

qa.q: How does Kwame feel about the questions?
qa.a: Kwame feels amused and patient, laughing at Chidi's endless whys.

grounding: Shows a young child asking repeated causal questions to understand how the world works.

passage:
At the kindergarten, the first monsoon rain came during story time. Uday, five, pressed his nose to the window.
"Ma'am, why does rain fall down and not up?"
Jyoti ma'am smiled. "What do you think?"
"Because clouds are heavy?"
"Close! Water gets heavy and falls."
"Why is water heavy?"
The whole class started asking. Jyoti ma'am took them to the veranda to watch the drops.

qa.q: Where did Jyoti ma'am take the class?
qa.a: To the veranda to watch the drops.

qa.q: How did Uday feel watching the first rain?
qa.a: He felt curious and eager, pressing his nose to the window.

qa.q: What did Jyoti ma'am do that encouraged curiosity?
qa.a: She asked what he thought first, then took the class outside to see.

qa.q: How might the other children feel after Uday's question?
qa.a: They seem excited and curious too, all starting to ask why.

grounding: Shows a young child's repeated why questions in a school setting.

passage:
I'm Amandeep, Joseph's older cousin. During the summer holidays, Joseph, who's five, followed me around asking why.
"Why do ants walk in a line?"
"Why is the sky blue?"
"Why does ice melt?"
I didn't know half the answers. So we tested ice melting on the steps. He watched it the whole time, then asked why it melted faster in the sun.
By evening I was exhausted. He was not.

qa.q: What did they test on the steps?
qa.a: Ice melting.

qa.q: How was Joseph feeling during the ice test?
qa.a: He felt fascinated and curious, watching the whole time.

qa.q: What was good about how Amandeep handled not knowing?
qa.a: Amandeep tested the question with Joseph instead of guessing, which fed his curiosity.

qa.q: How does Amandeep feel by evening?
qa.a: Amandeep feels exhausted but seems fond of Joseph's endless questions.

grounding: An older cousin describes a young child asking repeated why questions over the summer.

passage:
Tuesday: thick winter fog covered Delhi. Rajni, five, pressed her nose to the bus window. "Masi, why can't we see the trees?"
"Because of fog." "Why is there fog?" "Tiny drops of water in the air." "Why is the water in the air?"
Seema Masi laughed. "Let's find out."
Thursday: she boiled water and held a cold steel plate over the steam. Tiny drops appeared. Rajni gasped. "It's a baby cloud!"
Next Monday, the fog came again. Rajni told her cousin at the bus stop, "It's cold air making the water show up. Masi and I made some." Then, a moment later: "But why is air cold?"

qa.q: What did Seema Masi hold over the steam?
qa.a: She held a cold steel plate over the steam.

qa.q: What was Rajni feeling when drops appeared on the plate?
qa.a: She felt amazed and thrilled, gasping and calling it a baby cloud.

qa.q: How could an adult respond to a child's endless "why" questions?
qa.a: They can answer simply, admit when it's worth finding out together, and try small safe experiments, the way Seema Masi did.

qa.q: What would change if Seema Masi had told Rajni to stop asking?
qa.a: Rajni might have felt dismissed and stopped wondering, and she would have missed the fun of finding the answer herself.

grounding: Shows a young child asking chains of "why" questions to understand how fog works.
